subject: Mathematics
title: Complex Numbers
learningOutcomes: Recall a complex number as \(z=a+ib\) or the ordered pair \((a,b)\), where \(a,b\) are real and \(i=\sqrt{-1}\).
Identify \(a\) as the real part and \(b\) as the imaginary part of \(z\).
State and use the condition for the equality of two complex numbers.
Add, subtract, multiply and divide complex numbers, and represent them in the Argand plane.
Define the conjugate \(\bar z\) and use it to find the reciprocal and the quotient of complex numbers.
Find the modulus \(|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) and use \(z\bar z=|z|^2\).
Solve equations and systems of linear equations with complex coefficients.
Factorise and solve quadratic and simple cubic equations whose roots are complex.
Describe a point by polar coordinates \((r,\theta)\) and convert between polar and rectangular coordinates.
Find the argument and the principal argument \(\operatorname{Arg}z\in(-\pi,\pi]\) of a complex number.
Write a complex number in polar form \(r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)=re^{i\theta}\).
Multiply and divide complex numbers in polar form and use De Moivre's theorem for integer powers.
Describe simple loci in the Argand plane such as circles, perpendicular bisectors and rays.
Apply complex numbers to simple harmonic motion, impedance \(E=IZ\) and the addition of waves.
Find the real and imaginary parts of powers and quotients of complex numbers and write equations in \(x\) and \(y\).

sections.heading: Why Complex Numbers?
sections.body: No real number squares to \(-1\), so we introduce the imaginary unit \(i\) with \(i^2=-1\) (written \(i=\sqrt{-1}\)). For \(a>0\), \(\sqrt{-a}=i\sqrt{a}\); for example \(\sqrt{-25}=5i\). The powers of \(i\) repeat in a cycle of four: \(i,\,-1,\,-i,\,1,\,i,\ldots\), so to find \(i^n\) divide \(n\) by \(4\) and use the remainder.

sections.heading: The Complex Number and the Argand Plane
sections.body: A complex number is \(z=x+iy\) with \(x,y\) real. \(\operatorname{Re}z=x\) is the real part and \(\operatorname{Im}z=y\) (a real number, not \(iy\)) is the imaginary part. Two complex numbers are equal exactly when their real parts are equal and their imaginary parts are equal. Writing \(z\) as the ordered pair \((x,y)\) lets us plot it in the Argand plane, with the real axis horizontal and the imaginary axis vertical. Every real number is complex (\(x=x+0i\)), but complex numbers cannot be ordered with \(<\) and \(>\).

sections.heading: Basic Operations
sections.body: Add and subtract the real parts and the imaginary parts separately. Multiply with \((a+bi)(c+di)=(ac-bd)+(ad+bc)i\), using \(i^2=-1\). To divide, multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator so that the denominator becomes the real number \(c^2+d^2\): \(\dfrac{a+bi}{c+di}=\dfrac{(a+bi)(c-di)}{c^2+d^2}\). The sum of two complex numbers is the diagonal of the parallelogram on their vectors.

sections.heading: Conjugate and Modulus
sections.body: The conjugate of \(z=x+iy\) is \(\bar z=x-iy\), the mirror image of \(z\) in the real axis. Then \(z+\bar z=2x\), \(z-\bar z=2iy\) and \(z\bar z=x^2+y^2\). The modulus \(|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) is the distance of \(z\) from the origin, so \(|z|\ge0\) and \(|z|^2=z\bar z\). Useful rules: \(|z_1z_2|=|z_1||z_2|\), \(|\bar z|=|z|\) and \(|z_1+z_2|\le|z_1|+|z_2|\). The distance between \(z_1\) and \(z_2\) is \(|z_1-z_2|\).

sections.heading: Equations, Powers and Quadratics
sections.body: To find \(\operatorname{Re}\) or \(\operatorname{Im}\) of a power or a quotient, simplify it to the form \(a+bi\) first. An equation between complex numbers becomes two real equations: one for the real parts and one for the imaginary parts. A quadratic \(z^2+bz+c=0\) with real coefficients and \(D=b^2-4c<0\) has two non-real roots \(z=\dfrac{-b\pm i\sqrt{-D}}{2}\) that are conjugates of each other. Because \(z^2+a^2=(z+ai)(z-ai)\), sums of squares factorise over the complex numbers.

sections.heading: Polar Coordinates and Polar Form
sections.body: A point can be described by \((r,\theta)\) where \(r\) is its distance from the origin and \(\theta\) the angle from the positive x-axis. They are linked by \(x=r\cos\theta\), \(y=r\sin\theta\), \(r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) and \(\tan\theta=y/x\). The argument of \(z\) is any such \(\theta\) (all differ by multiples of \(2\pi\)); the principal argument \(\operatorname{Arg}z\) is the one in \((-\pi,\pi]\). Find the quadrant first, because \(\tan^{-1}(y/x)\) alone is only correct when \(x>0\). The polar form is \(z=r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)=re^{i\theta}\) (Euler's formula).

sections.heading: Products, Quotients and Powers in Polar Form
sections.body: If \(z_1=r_1(\cos\theta_1+i\sin\theta_1)\) and \(z_2=r_2(\cos\theta_2+i\sin\theta_2)\), then \(z_1z_2=r_1r_2\big[\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2)+i\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2)\big]\) and \(\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}=\dfrac{r_1}{r_2}\big[\cos(\theta_1-\theta_2)+i\sin(\theta_1-\theta_2)\big]\): multiply or divide the moduli, add or subtract the arguments. Repeated multiplication gives De Moivre's theorem \((\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)^n=\cos n\theta+i\sin n\theta\). The arguments add only up to a multiple of \(2\pi\), so bring the result back into \((-\pi,\pi]\) if you need the principal argument.

sections.heading: Loci in the Argand Plane
sections.body: \(|z-z_0|=r\) is the circle with centre \(z_0\) and radius \(r\). \(|z-z_1|=|z-z_2|\) is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining \(z_1\) and \(z_2\). \(\operatorname{Re}z=k\) is the vertical line \(x=k\) and \(\operatorname{Im}z=k\) is the horizontal line \(y=k\). \(\operatorname{Arg}z=\alpha\) is a ray from the origin. To find the equation of a locus, put \(z=x+iy\), square both sides and simplify.

sections.heading: Applications
sections.body: Complex numbers describe simple harmonic motion: the displacement is \(x=x_{max}e^{i\theta}\), or \(x=x_{max}e^{i\omega t}\) with \(\omega=2\pi f\). In an AC circuit the voltage \(E\), current \(I\) and impedance \(Z\) satisfy \(E=IZ\); the impedance of a resistor is the real number \(R\). Electrical engineers write \(j\) for the imaginary unit because \(i\) stands for current. To add two waves, write each as the real part of a complex number, add the complex numbers, and read the new amplitude and phase from the modulus and argument of the sum.

definitions.definition: A number \(z=x+iy\) with \(x,y\) real, or the ordered pair \((x,y)\).
A complex number whose real part is \(0\) and whose imaginary part is not \(0\), such as \(5i\).
The plane in which \(x+iy\) is the point \((x,y)\); the real part is horizontal and the imaginary part vertical.
\(\bar z=x-iy\), the mirror image of \(z\) in the real axis; \(z\bar z=x^2+y^2\).
\(|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\), the distance of \(z\) from the origin.
\((r,\theta)\): the distance from the origin and the angle from the positive x-axis, with \(x=r\cos\theta\) and \(y=r\sin\theta\).
The angle \(\theta\) of the polar coordinates of \(z\); it is determined up to a multiple of \(2\pi\).
The value of the argument in the interval \((-\pi,\pi]\), written \(\operatorname{Arg}z\).
The complex quantity \(Z\) in an AC circuit with \(E=IZ\); for a resistor \(Z=R\).

examTips: To find \(i^n\), divide \(n\) by \(4\) and use the remainder: \(0\to1,\ 1\to i,\ 2\to-1,\ 3\to-i\).
\(\operatorname{Im}(3+4i)=4\), not \(4i\): the imaginary part is a real number.
To divide, multiply the top and the bottom by the conjugate of the denominator; the denominator becomes the real number \(c^2+d^2\).
\(|x+iy|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\). Do not add \(x\) and \(y\), and do not forget the square root.
For the argument, locate the quadrant first. \(\tan^{-1}(y/x)\) is correct only when \(x>0\); for \(x<0\) add or subtract \(\pi\) and keep the answer in \((-\pi,\pi]\).
In polar form multiply the moduli and add the arguments; divide the moduli and subtract the arguments.
For \(|z-z_1|=|z-z_2|\), put \(z=x+iy\), square both sides and simplify: it is always a straight line.
